We have proton NMR data: peaks at 2.62 (t, J=7.3 Hz, 2H), 2.77 (t, J=7.3 Hz, 2H), aromatic region: 7.18 (ddd, 2H), 7.36 (ddd, 2H). So total integration: 2+2+2+2 = 8 H. Aromatic 4 H suggests a para-disubstituted benzene (AA'BB' pattern). Two aliphatic CH2 groups each 2H as triplets coupling to each other (J=7.3). Likely ethyl chain attached to aromatic ring on each side? Actually a para-disubstituted benzene with two ethyl groups? That would be p-diethylbenzene: C6H4(C2H5)2. That has aromatic 4 H, two ethyl groups each CH2-CH3. But we only see two CH2 signals (2.62 and 2.77) each 2H, but no methyl signals (~1.2 ppm). So maybe the ethyl groups are attached to heteroatoms? Actually CH2-CH2 attached to aromatic? Could be phenethyl? But that would have CH2 next to aromatic (~2.7) and CH2 next to something else (~2.6). But we have only 4 aliphatic H total, not 4+? Phenethyl has CH2-CH2-Ph: CH2 next to aromatic ~2.7 (2H), CH2 next to something else maybe attached to something else? But we have two triplets each 2H, suggests a -CH2-CH2- chain symmetrical? Could be para-xylene? No.

Consider p-xylylene? Actually p-xylylene (para-phenylene) with two CH2 groups attached to benzene (i.e., 1,4-bis(methylene)benzene). That would be C6H4(CH2)2, each CH2 attached directly to aromatic, giving signals around 2.9 maybe as singlets? But they are triplets, indicating each CH2 coupled to the other CH2 (i.e., -CH2-CH2- bridging). So structure: benzene ring with -CH2-CH2- substituents at para positions, forming a 1,4-bis(ethane)?? Actually that would be p-phenylene with ethyl groups? Wait: If we have para-disubstituted benzene with -CH2-CH2- groups attached to ring, each group is -CH2-CH2- (ethyl) attached to ring at one end. The CH2 attached to ring (benzylic) appears around 2.6-2.8, the other CH2 (next to something else) appears similar. They are coupled to each other (triplet). So each ethyl group gives two triplets (CH2-CH2). Integration 2H each, total 4H per ethyl, but we have only 4 aliphatic H total, meaning only one ethyl group? But we have two triplets each 2H, total 4H, which could be from a single ethyl group (CH2-CH2) but that would be CH2-CH2-? Actually ethyl group is CH3-CH2-; we would see a quartet (CH2) and a triplet (CH3). Not two triplets. So it's a -CH2-CH2- chain attached at both ends to aromatic? That would be a para-phenylene ethylene bridging? That is 1,4-bis(ethylene)benzene? Actually structure: benzene with -CH2-CH2- substituents at para positions, each substituent is -CH2-CH2- (ethyl) attached to ring at the CH2 nearest ring. So each substituent has CH2 (benzylic) and CH2 (terminal). The terminal CH2 would be attached to nothing else? It would be CH2-? Actually it's -CH2-CH3? No, if it's ethyl attached to ring, it's -CH2-CH3. That gives CH3 triplet, not CH2. So not.

If we have -CH2-CH2- attached to ring at both ends, that would be a -CH2-CH2- bridging between two para positions? That would be a 1,4-phenylene ethylene (i.e., 1,4-bis(ethylene)benzene) which is actually a cyclohexadiene? Not.

Maybe the compound is p-xylene? No aliphatic.

Let's search NMR database with these peaks.
